input.heading: Source Chapter: The Memantine AD Study (academic, fictionalized)

output.executive_summary: Alzheimer's disease affects approximately 55 million people worldwide according to the World Health Organization. The progressive neurodegeneration leads to memory loss, cognitive decline, and ultimately the loss of independent living. Memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, has been approved for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's since 2003.
bullet_points: Alzheimer's disease affects approximately 55 million people worldwide according to the World Health Organization.
The progressive neurodegeneration leads to memory loss, cognitive decline, and ultimately the loss of independent living.
Memantine, an NMDA receptor antagonist, has been approved for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's since 2003.
Memantine functions as a low-affinity, non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist.
The drug blocks the excitotoxic effects of glutamate while preserving normal physiological neurotransmission.
This selective blockade is achieved through the drug's low affinity, which allows it to bind during pathologically elevated glutamate levels but dissociate during normal synaptic transmission.
Researchers demonstrated that memantine reduces calcium influx into neurons by approximately 40%.
The study found that this reduction prevents the downstream cascade of tau phosphorylation and amyloid accumulation.
A 24-week randomized controlled trial enrolled 252 patients with moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease.
The results demonstrated that memantine treatment led to a 50% improvement in cognitive scores compared to placebo.
